maps.name: Using the library self-checkout station
maps.context: A student uses a self-checkout station to borrow several books before leaving the university library.
maps.notes: The interaction combines physical books, a touchscreen, a barcode scanner, a payment-style confirmation sound, and a printed receipt. The student is familiar with self-checkout systems but not this particular interface.

rows.description: The angled touchscreen, scanner surface, and open space beside the screen suggest that the student can place and interact with objects at the station.
signifiers: Printed outline showing where to place a book

rows.description: The screen clearly identifies the station as a borrowing system, but the first required action is not immediately obvious because several buttons have similar visual weight.
rows.change: Make the first action visually dominant and reduce competing options.

rows.description: The button appears actionable because of its border, placement, and label. However, the nearby “Language” and “Help” controls look almost identical.
rows.change: Give the primary action a clearer hierarchy than secondary controls.
signifiers: Position at the centre of the screen

rows.description: The student understands that the barcode must be placed over the scanner, but the relationship between the book orientation and the scanner area is unclear.
rows.change: Show the expected book orientation directly beside the scanner.

rows.description: A short sound occurs after a successful scan and the book title appears on screen. When the scan fails, the system produces no sound and only a small text message.
rows.change: Use a distinct response for failed scans and make the error state more noticeable.

rows.description: The scanned book appears in the list, but the student has to scroll to confirm that multiple books have been added.
rows.change: Keep the number of scanned items and the latest item visible without scrolling.

rows.description: The student can remove a scanned book, but the control is only available after opening a secondary menu. This prevents accidental removal but makes correction slow.
rows.change: Expose a clear undo action immediately after each scan.

rows.description: The student expects the large green button labelled “Finish” to complete the borrowing process. Instead, it advances to a second confirmation screen.
rows.change: Rename the button to indicate the next state, or combine the two confirmation steps.

rows.description: The confirmation screen displays a receipt icon and a short message, but it does not state whether the books are now successfully borrowed.
rows.change: Use explicit completion language and show the due date.

rows.description: The receipt slot is physically visible, but the relationship between printing the receipt and completing the borrowing process is not clear.
rows.change: Clarify that the receipt is optional and that borrowing is already complete.
signifiers: Text explaining that the receipt is optional

rows.description: The touchscreen uses blue confirmation controls while the physical scanner uses green lighting. The different visual cues make it unclear whether both refer to the same successful state.
rows.change: Use a consistent success cue across the screen, scanner and receipt area.
